summary: A USB 1.x/2.0 inline sniffer built on a FriendlyElec NanoPi NEO Air single-board computer (Allwinner H3), confirmed directly in the vendor's own documentation. Instead of dedicated capture silicon (FPGA/CPLD) like the other sniffers in this category, it does USB passthrough and packet capture entirely in software on the SBC's Linux kernel, then lets you pull PCAP files or control it remotely over WiFi/SSH.
honest_take: This is essentially a ~$15-20 Allwinner H3 Linux SBC marked up roughly 10x, with the real value being the vendor's custom 'software passthrough' capture stack rather than any special hardware. That software approach is also its biggest limitation: the vendor's own docs explicitly warn against connecting a USB flash drive because it can't keep up with sustained bulk transfers - something a hardware FPGA sniffer wouldn't struggle with. 'Remote control' is genuinely just SSH and a cloud web portal into a Linux box, and the device must stay network-connected to capture at all, which undercuts any 'portable field tool' framing. An independent reviewer (Doug Brown's blog) also flagged unclear language suggesting cloud registration might be required even for local use.

name: OpticSpy
firmware_note: No microcontroller and nothing to flash. OpticSpy is a fixed analog signal chain (photodiode -> two op-amp gain stages -> comparator) feeding an FTDI USB-to-UART bridge chip. Full schematics, BOM, and Gerbers are published by Grand Idea Studio under CC-BY-3.0.
price_note: Confirmed live on Crowd Supply as of check date (In stock), plus $8 US / $18 worldwide shipping. Originally a Crowd Supply crowdfunding campaign (launched Feb 2018, NOT Kickstarter) and has remained continuously available/in stock since.
skill_note: Outputs a raw NRZ digital bitstream with no onboard decoding. You manually tune two gain potentiometers and then capture/decode the signal yourself (logic analyzer, sigrok, custom script) - it is not a point-and-click IR/optical decoder.
build_note: Fully assembled, tested module with a built-in FTDI FT231XS-R USB-to-UART bridge (confirmed in the official bill of materials), so it plugs directly into a host USB port and enumerates as a serial device. Decoding whatever bitstream you receive is entirely on you.
summary: An open-source (CC-BY-3.0) analog photodiode receiver module from Grand Idea Studio (Joe Grand), sold continuously on Crowd Supply since its February 2018 campaign. A Vishay BPW21R silicon photodiode feeds two Maxim op-amp gain stages and a Maxim comparator to turn a visible-light or near-IR optical signal into a raw digital serial bitstream, exposed to a host PC over USB via an onboard FTDI chip.
honest_take: This is essentially Maxim's own decades-old application-note reference circuit (AN1117, 'Small Photodiode Receiver Handles Fiber-Optic Data Rates to 800kbps') built onto a nice open PCB with an FTDI chip added for USB convenience - there is no microcontroller, no signal processing, and no decoding logic on board at all. It cites the classic Loughry & Umphress 'optical TEMPEST' paper as inspiration, but OpticSpy itself is not a TEMPEST-grade eavesdropping tool: no directional optics, no long-range sensitivity - the vendor's own range tests only reached about 1-3 inches. It's a hobbyist-range receiver front end, full stop, and you still have to build or find your own decoder for whatever signal you're chasing.

Decoding IR remote controls and other near-IR blink codes with your own software
Learning analog photodiode receiver design from a real, fully documented reference circuit
not_for: Long-range or directional TEMPEST-style optical eavesdropping - range is inches, not meters, in the vendor's own tests

High-bandwidth optical links - hard-capped around 800kbps by the underlying app-note design

name: Socket Target for CW308 (STM32F-SOCKET64)
firmware_note: Ships with no firmware at all. It's an empty socket; whatever STM32F chip you drop in runs whatever test firmware you flash yourself (e.g. ChipWhisperer's bundled AES/crypto test binaries).
price_note: Board only. No MCU included, and it does NOT work standalone - it requires a CW308 UFO baseboard (NewAE part NAE-CW308-04), which is sold separately and not bundled with this listing. Total buy-in is well above $140 for a first-time buyer.
skill_note: You're expected to already run ChipWhisperer, own a CW308 UFO baseboard, and be comfortable hand-placing a bare TQFP-64 chip and picking the right pinout-switch position for your specific STM32F part.
build_note: No soldering to use it - it's a zero-insertion-force (ZIF) socket, drop the chip in and close the lever. But it only becomes a working setup once seated on a CW308 UFO baseboard you already own.
summary: A CW308-family daughtercard that is nothing but an empty TQFP-64 ZIF socket, a 2-position switch to select between two STM32F pinout families (chips with an onboard voltage regulator like STM32F415, vs. chips without like STM32F303), and routing to the CW308 20-pin connector. It exists so a researcher can side-channel or fault-inject an arbitrary user-supplied STM32F part without designing a custom carrier PCB for every chip.
honest_take: This is a passive accessory, not a tool - it doesn't glitch or measure anything itself, it's the thing that gets glitched by an external ChipWhisperer (or similar) attacking it through the CW308 baseboard. It is genuinely useless on its own: no MCU is included, and it will not connect to anything without a CW308 UFO baseboard, which NewAE sells separately and which most buyers don't already own unless they're already deep into the ChipWhisperer ecosystem. If you're not already a CW308 UFO owner, buying this $140 socket card first is backwards - budget for the baseboard too before you order this. This record is deliberately capability-sparse: it is a passive chip socket with no independent function of its own, and that sparseness is the finding, not an oversight.

not_for: Anyone without an existing CW308 UFO baseboard - this card cannot be used standalone
Beginners - ships with zero MCU and no guided workflow

The listed core voltage (1.2V) is not actually delivered by an onboard regulator for testing purposes - NewAE bypasses the SAM4S's internal regulator and feeds 1.2V in externally from the baseboard's LDO specifically so the power trace is clean, which is a deliberate side-channel-friendly design choice, not a limitation, but it means this board cannot run on its own supply rail either. Like the CW308 socket target in this same batch, this is a legitimately sparse device - it is a fixed target board, not a multi-function tool, and the short capability list reflects that rather than shallow research.

firmware_note: Single official open-source firmware (Apache-2.0, third-party components GPL-3.0/Apache-2.0) built on ESP-IDF v5.5; bundles a BlackMagic Probe GDB server, a CherryDAP CMSIS-DAP stack, an XVC server, and the logic-analyzer/UART-bridge web backend into one image, updated OTA or over USB.

summary: ESP32JTAG is a wireless debug probe from Canadian startup EZ32 Inc.: an ESP32-S3 running open-source firmware (BlackMagic Probe GDB server + CMSIS-DAP via CherryDAP) paired with a small Lattice iCE40UP5K FPGA that does the high-speed signal capture for a 16-channel logic analyzer and FPGA bitstream programming (Xilinx Virtual Cable). Everything - JTAG/SWD debugging, the logic analyzer, a UART terminal, and firmware updates - is driven through a built-in HTTPS web server reached over Wi-Fi, so there's no USB driver install.
honest_take: Wireless JTAG is a real engineering tradeoff, not a free upgrade: Wi-Fi adds latency and jitter a wired USB-HS probe (hs-probe, a J-Link, or even a $15 clone) doesn't have, and for tight real-time debugging that shows up as slower round-trips no matter how good the raw throughput numbers look. The vendor's own comparison table also lists 'Wi-Fi 6' connectivity, but the ESP32-S3's radio is 802.11 b/g/n (Wi-Fi 4) only - the silicon has no 802.11ax hardware, so that line is either a spec-sheet error or marketing inflation; treat the rest of that comparison table skeptically too. It's also a debug probe running an HTTPS web server on your Wi-Fi network with no documented authentication - on a shared or IoT-segment network that's an open control/flash surface for anyone who can reach its IP. The 16-channel/250MHz logic analyzer plus driver-free multi-tool angle is a genuinely strong pitch, since the iCE40UP5K FPGA is doing real work, this is not 'just an ESP32 in a case'. But for latency-sensitive production debugging, a wired probe is still the safer default.

firmware_note: Pure-Rust CMSIS-DAP v1/v2 implementation written for this specific board; only one tagged release (0.1.4, Aug 2021) though source commits continued to late 2023. A 'turbo' build flag overclocks the STM32F723 from 72 MHz to 216 MHz.

summary: hs-probe is an open-hardware SWD/JTAG debug probe built around an STM32F723 (Cortex-M7 with an integrated USB 2.0 High-Speed PHY), designed for the probe-rs project. It enumerates as a CMSIS-DAP v1/v2 probe over genuine USB-HS (480 Mbit/s) rather than the USB Full-Speed (12 Mbit/s) most CMSIS-DAP probes are limited to, and includes a USB mux so the STM32's bootloader stays reachable for firmware recovery. Hardware is CERN-OHL-P v2 licensed with published schematics; firmware is dual Apache-2.0/MIT.
honest_take: For most hobbyist STM32/nRF work, a $15 CMSIS-DAP clone or a Raspberry Pi Pico running DAPLink firmware will flash and debug just as well - the difference only shows up when you're moving real data over the wire: high-rate SWO tracing, big flash writes, or RTT-style logging, where hs-probe's genuine USB-HS link is meaningfully faster. What the project's own materials undersell: the firmware source has a full jtag.rs module, so JTAG is implemented even though probe-rs's docs and the Tindie listing both lean almost entirely on 'SWD probe' framing. The bigger concern is the project itself: the hardware repo hasn't been touched since January 2022, firmware commits stopped in November 2023 with 11 issues still open, there's been only one tagged firmware release ever (2021), and the Tindie shop isn't taking orders. It still works today because CMSIS-DAP is a stable protocol and the parent probe-rs debugging software keeps supporting it, but don't expect the hs-probe hardware/firmware itself to see more attention. This is a genuinely single-purpose device (SWD/JTAG only, nothing else) - the short capability list below is a real finding about the product, not a research gap.

firmware_note: No reflashable on-board firmware - the board is built around WCH's CH347 USB-to-multi-protocol bridge chip, a fixed-function IC. summary: BRUSCHETTA Board is Luca Bongiorni's (WHID Injector) open, assembled multi-protocol debugger built around WCH's CH347 USB bridge chip, wired for UART, JTAG/SWD (via a Bongiorni-patched OpenOCD build), I2C (EEPROM read/write via his ch347eeprom tool), and SPI (including flash chip dumping via flashrom's ch347_spi driver). A DIP switch selects between two main modes (UART+I2C+SPI, or UART+JTAG) and jumper-selectable level shifters cover 1.8V-5V targets.
honest_take: This sits in the exact niche already covered by Bus Pirate 5 and Tigard in this database, and it doesn't clearly beat either. It's built on a single off-the-shelf WCH CH347 bridge chip rather than a general-purpose MCU (Bus Pirate 5 uses an RP2040) or a dedicated FTDI part (Tigard uses an FT2232H), and its protocols are split across two DIP-switch-selected modes rather than all available simultaneously - you have to physically flip the switch and unplug I2C/SPI devices before using it as a JTAG debugger. The GitHub repo has had no commits since October 2024, is maintained by one person, and carries no license file. The genuine draw is that it's Luca Bongiorni's own board with his own OpenOCD fork already patched for CH347 and flashrom support baked in, and it undercuts Tigard on price - a reasonable pick if you're already using his WHID toolset, but not an obvious upgrade over the probes already tracked here.

name: DigiLab for FlipperZero
firmware_note: Official companion Flipper Application Package (FAP), open source (GPL-3.0), runs on stock Flipper Zero firmware and is listed in Flipper's official app catalog. All signal processing (ring buffers, statistical analysis, frequency detection) runs on the Flipper's own STM32WB55, not on the DigiLab module itself.
price_note: $64 USD confirmed via Lab401's US storefront (Shop Pay listing); Lab401's EU-facing page lists EUR 49 (~£42 GBP) - currency shown depends on storefront region.
skill_note: Designed to be approachable: guided in-app calibration, and voltage/protocol info is surfaced via audio/LED/haptic feedback rather than requiring the user to read raw numbers or scope traces.
build_note: Plugs directly onto the Flipper Zero's GPIO header, no soldering; comes with mini-probes for desktop use and a probe tip for portable use.
summary: DigiLab is a Flipper Zero GPIO add-on designed by tixlegeek for Lab401: a probe module with its own analog front-end (protection/conditioning circuitry rated to 12V, plus an onboard I2C EEPROM used for demos) that feeds signals to the Flipper's own CPU rather than carrying a separate processor. The open-source (GPL-3.0) companion app provides four tools: an oscilloscope-style Scope with configurable audio/LED/haptic feedback, a quick voltage/frequency Probe, and I2C/SPI device scanners with a built-in hex editor for reading and writing device registers.
honest_take: This is not just a GPIO pin breakout: Lab401's own behind-the-scenes post says they tried and abandoned putting an ESP32 on the board, and shipped analog signal-conditioning circuitry (voltage scaling/protection up to 12V) plus an onboard demo EEPROM instead - there is genuine purpose-built hardware behind the $64. That said, most of what makes it interesting - the oscilloscope view, the configurable feedback, the I2C/SPI 'prediction engine' - is software running entirely on the Flipper's own CPU, so DigiLab itself is best understood as a well-engineered analog probe front-end for the Flipper's GPIO. It also caps out at ~200kHz and is 3.3V-only for its I2C/SPI modes, so it's explicitly pitched as a first-look exploration tool rather than a scope or logic-analyzer replacement. It does NOT add any of the Flipper's headline radio capabilities (Sub-GHz, NFC/RFID, IR) - those come from the Flipper itself and are unrelated to this module, a common point of confusion for anyone assuming a Flipper 'module' adds radio range or protocols.

name: FlatSat – DEFCON 34
firmware_note: Preloaded, intentionally vulnerable AMP (asymmetric multiprocessing) firmware split across the RP2040's two Cortex-M0+ cores - one core runs the simulated spacecraft bus/telemetry stack, the other handles LoRa radio timing. Eight numbered attack walkthroughs (00-07) cover packet fuzzing, telecommand spoofing, buffer overflows, and subsystem manipulation.
price_note: Confirmed out of stock directly on the Electronic Cats DEFCON 34 store page as of check date. This edition includes an exclusive DEF CON 34 commemorative patch on top of the base board.
skill_note: Marketed as needing 'no soldering or coding initially' (drag-and-drop firmware, guided 3-level CTF), but the actual attack walkthroughs (buffer overflows, telecommand spoofing, RF protocol analysis) assume real binary-exploitation and RF fundamentals.
build_note: Ships as a complete, assembled board; setup is USB connect + firmware drag-and-drop. No soldering needed to start the CTF.
summary: An RP2040-based training board built around two Semtech SX1262 LoRa radios and a BME280/LIS2DH12 sensor pair, preloaded with deliberately vulnerable firmware that mimics a small satellite's telemetry/command bus. Originally an independent open-source project published by researcher(s) as Pwnsat, this DEFCON 34 edition is a limited commemorative production run manufactured and sold by Electronic Cats (an established open-hardware company) from a fork of the original Pwnsat/FlatSat GitHub repo.
honest_take: The RP2040 and SX1262 radios are real and confirmed, and the underlying Pwnsat project has genuine traction (500+ GitHub stars, active commits) - this isn't vaporware. But 'analyze LoRa telemetry with an SDR' oversells what's onboard: FlatSat's own radios are fixed-function SX1262 LoRa transceivers, not an SDR - you bring your own RTL-SDR/HackRF to passively watch the RF side; the board itself doesn't do general-purpose signal capture. Also worth knowing before buying: when checked, the project's own GitHub wiki pages (hardware anatomy, attack walkthroughs) all returned load errors - the polished front page currently oversells docs that weren't fully working. It's out of stock at Electronic Cats regardless, so hobbyist interest is currently better served by building from the open Pwnsat/FlatSat repo directly than waiting on the commemorative edition.

If you want the finished tool, the vendor's own 'PRO' kit bundles all of that (plus a case) for $185, which is the realistic all-in price of a working Fire Weasel; this listing is for people who already own the modules (e.g. from a previous CYD build) and just want a proper carrier board and strap instead of a breadboard. name: Sword of Secrets
firmware_note: Ships pre-flashed with the first challenge stages. Bootloader is locked by default so only officially encrypted updates can be flashed over USB; an 'open bootloader' fully-hackable variant was announced as a funding stretch goal but delivery could not be confirmed from the campaign's public update log.
price_note: Crowd Supply lists $45 for the board plus $8 US / $18 worldwide shipping, confirmed in stock ('ships within three business days') as of check date. A campaign update warned the post-campaign retail price would be higher than the $45 crowdfunding price, but $45 remains the live listed price.
skill_note: Solving stages requires reading datasheets, RISC-V assembly/firmware-level work, and spotting cryptographic implementation flaws - the vendor markets it to 'security researchers, enthusiasts, educators', not total beginners, though a free browser-based emulator lets you preview challenges before buying.
build_note: Fully assembled, plugs directly into USB (includes a shim to thicken the onboard USB Type-A connector for a snug fit). New content arrives as encrypted USB firmware updates, not hardware changes.
summary: A keychain-sized, sword-shaped PCB built around a WCH CH32V003 RISC-V microcontroller, a Winbond W25Q128 SPI NOR flash chip, and a CH340E USB-serial bridge, packaged as a multi-stage hardware CTF. Made by Israeli embedded-security researcher Gili Yankovitch under Nyx Software Security Solutions, it shipped its first production batch of 250 units in Dec 2025-Jan 2026 after a 969%-funded Crowd Supply campaign, and the vendor has committed to shipping new encrypted challenge stages over USB for at least a year post-fulfillment.
honest_take: The brief's framing of this as 'successor to The Skull CTF by the same maker' needs correcting: Crowd Supply's own page calls it a 'spiritual successor to Uri Shaked's The Skull CTF' - same genre of hardware-puzzle badge, but a different maker entirely (Gili Yankovitch/Nyx vs. Uri Shaked/Wokwi). Don't expect direct continuity of challenges, design, or team between the two. On the hardware: the CH32V003 is a real, extremely cheap (~$0.10-0.15 in volume) RISC-V MCU - the campaign itself jokes about building a secure update mechanism around 'a 10-cent MCU' - so the $45 price is mostly paying for the puzzle design, the encrypted content pipeline, and the promise of ongoing new stages, not exotic silicon. That's a legitimate thing to pay for if the challenge content is good (open firmware and hardware files back that up), but go in knowing you're buying curated content and a subscription-style update stream on commodity hardware, not a beefier board than a Skull or a DVID.
